Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 95, verses 1–3:

Allah has sworn by the fig, the olive, Mount Sinai and the secure city of Makkah, in connection with the natural disposition (fitrah) of man, which is upright. This oath serves as a suitable and fitting frame for that reality, which is the nature of man. We have already established earlier that between the reality whose picture is to be framed by the oaths sworn by the sights of nature and those sights there is a particular correspondence, which is in some places clear and in some places very subtle and intricate.

By "Tur Sinin" is meant the mountain at whose foot Allah and Musa (peace be upon him) held their discourse, and by "al-balad al-amin" is meant the city of Makkah. The connection of these two places with religious truths is entirely clear. As for the fig and the olive, their connection is not apparent on the surface: what their relationship is to the natural disposition of man, to the creation of man, or to religious truths.

There are many narrations and sayings concerning the interpretation of the fig (tin) and the olive (zaytun). Some sayings state that "Tin" refers to the place called "Tutaynah", which is near Damascus. Others said that the fig refers to the tree whose leaves Adam and Hawwa (peace be upon them both) wrapped around their bodies, when, after being deceived by Satan in the Garden, they were deprived of their clothing; and after this both were sent down to the earth and began life here. Some sayings interpret it as the mountain on which Noah's Ark came to rest and settled, in which fig trees grew abundantly.

Many sayings have been related concerning the olive. According to some, it refers to "Tur Zaita", which is in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Others said that it refers to Bayt al-Maqdis itself. Others said that it refers to the branch of olive which the dove brought, which Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him) released from the Ark, so that he might learn the state of the flood: when the dove came with an olive branch, he came to know that the water had receded from some parts of the earth and that trees had sprouted there.

Some scholars hold that the fig and the olive refer to the very fruits that we eat and know, and that no symbolic meaning is intended by them, or if there is any, it is only the places where they grow. These were the sayings. As for the olive, the Qur'an mentions it in other places too, that it grows on the mountain of Tur.

﴿And a tree that springs from Mount Sinai, producing oil and a relish for those who eat﴾ (23:20). And in Surah Abasa: ﴿And olives and palm trees﴾ (80:29). Whereas the fig is mentioned in the entire Qur'an only in this place.

Therefore, concerning any one of the above sayings we cannot make a definitive statement. However, keeping in view the manner of the Qur'an in matters of oaths, we can say that the reference of the fig and the olive is to places or events that are connected with religion and faith, or to what the answer of the oath states, that We created man in the best of forms. Perhaps the place intended is the paradise where man began his life, so that this indication of the two oaths also harmonises with the general manner of the Qur'an, and this frame becomes in harmony with the picture that it contains. In terms of the subject, the matter stated in the surah is this:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 95, verse 4:

This shows that from the very beginning of creation Allah made man in the best of forms, and that Allah's gracious attention has always been upon the human being. Although Allah has created everything in the best form, the mention here and elsewhere of the proportion of the human form, and of the balancing (taswiyah) and the due proportion (ta'dil) of man's limbs, is a sign that man holds great importance in the sight of Allah among His creatures. This is despite the fact that man has many weaknesses, that he strays from the right path, abandons the natural way and walks on wrong paths, and becomes entangled in evil and corruption. Even so, this attention from Allah shows that man has a station and rank in the sight of Allah, and that this station and rank lies within the whole system of this universe. That is why Allah has described the creation and form of man as being of the highest degree. Physically, this creature possesses a most complete and intricate system; intellectually also it surpasses all creation; and in terms of spiritual perfections it is also remarkably distinguished and accomplished.

Here greater importance is given to the spiritual aspect of man. For if man, in his spiritual dimension, abandons the natural path, falls into wrong ways, and chooses disbelief instead of faith, he falls very low; he sinks below all creatures. This is because man cannot change his physical structure; if he falls to the lowest level, he falls in the spiritual sense.

It is these spiritual qualities upon which man's superiority over all other creatures is based. By virtue of these qualities man is capable of rising to a station higher even than the honoured angels. The account of the Night Journey (Mi'raj) is evidence of this: Jibril (peace be upon him) went as far as a certain station and then stopped, while Muhammad (ﷺ) passed beyond that station, to very great heights and exalted degrees. And this same creature, man, if he falls, falls to a depth to which no other creature falls.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 95, verse 5:

﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low.﴾ (95:5) He was brought down to such a depth that even the beasts appeared higher than him. Compared with such humans, they appeared to be on the right path, because they remain upon their nature (fitrah), they are inspired to glorify and declare the oneness of God (tasbih and tahlil), and they continue to fulfill the purpose for which they were created on this earth. Yet this human was created in the finest form compared with other animals, but he denied his Lord and fell into so deep a pit that no further depth or degradation remained beyond it.

﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature.﴾ (95:4) That is, in terms of his nature and his capacities, he was the best.

﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low.﴾ (95:5) When he dropped his nature from the level that the Lord had set for him, and had made clear that below this line lies degradation and above it lies humanity and fitrah.

Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is a reward never to be cut off. (Qur'an 95:6)

Here the people referred to are those who remain firmly upon the path of fitrah (the natural disposition), and who, through faith and righteous action, fulfil the demands of their fitrah, and then attain the perfection that has been decreed for them, until they become the most perfect of the perfect. For such people:

﴿For them is a reward never to be cut off﴾. That is, a reward that is everlasting, neither interrupted nor severed. As for those who debase their fitrah downward, step by step, they keep falling further down, until they reach the lowest rank of Hell, where the last sign of their humanity also vanishes and they become embodied baseness.

The highest of the high (ʿIlliyyin) and the lowest of the low (Asfal Safilin) are in truth two extreme positions, and both begin from the straight line of fitrah. From the station of fitrah, a person keeps rising through faith and righteous action, and rising, reaches his appointed station, the Garden of Bliss (Jannat Naʿim). And if a person deviates from fitrah, keeps descending, and severs his bond with spirituality, then on reaching Hell he falls into its lowest level.

From this it becomes clear what the worth of faith is in human life. It is that light by whose illumination a person reaches a lofty station. Faith is the rope that serves as the link between human fitrah and its Creator, and it is that light in whose radiance the person advances step by step toward the station prepared for the most honoured people.

When this connection is broken, when this lamp is extinguished, the result is that humanity falls into a very deep pit and keeps falling; humanity sinks even below the animals. The human being remains merely an idol of clay, and then, like a stone, becomes fuel for Hell. In this atmosphere and environment, a call comes to the human being:

"O Prophet, in light of these realities, could any reasonable person deny you regarding the belief in the Hereafter? Especially since the value of humanity and the great station of faith are such, and once it is known how vile is the end of those who do not believe, who are deprived of light and from whose hands the firm rope of Allah has slipped away."

﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ (95:8). That is, is He not the greatest judge, when He judges among people in this manner? Is not the end of the believers and this end of the disbelievers based upon perfect wisdom? The justice is manifest, and the wisdom is exceedingly lofty. This is why it is related in a marfu' hadith from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that when one of you recites Surah At-Tin and Az-Zaytun and reaches the end and has recited:

﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ (95:8), then he should say: "Yes, and I am among those who bear witness to this."
